book_title: 7 Powers: The Foundations of Business Strategy

frameworks.name: Benefit/Barrier advantage test (barrier first, per competitor)
frameworks.decision: Does the business have a durable advantage that growth can come from, or is its edge copyable execution?
evidence_required: the claimed edge in the owner's words
customer evidence that it raises price, lowers cost or lowers investment (Benefit)
named competitors: direct, functional (substitutes, DIY) and likely entrants
why each competitor can't or won't copy it (Barrier)
retention, price premium or cost data if available
prerequisites: a defined offer and segment (one strategically separate business at a time)

branches.if: Benefit evidenced and a Barrier of a named type holds against every relevant competitor
branches.then: record the Power type; growth plan may lean on it (e.g. price, retention or acquisition spend sized to it)

branches.if: Benefit evidenced but no Barrier (rivals could copy within months)
branches.then: classify as execution advantage; keep it, but size investments to short payback and reversible commitments

branches.if: Barrier holds against incumbents but not against similar small rivals
branches.then: partial advantage; name the competitor it fails against and what would close the gap

branches.if: no Benefit evidence
branches.then: advantage unknown; research task (interviews, win/loss) before any claim

steps: Write the claimed edge
Name the Barrier first: scale cost of share gains, network, collateral damage, switching cost, brand history, fiat, process time
Check materiality (would it move price, cost or retention noticeably?)
Test against each competitor class
Record evidence source for each element
Label result: Power type / execution advantage / unknown
exceptions_failure_modes: Calling 'great service' or 'fast response' a moat
Treating a list of features as a Barrier
Judging only against the biggest incumbent and ignoring copycat small rivals
Applying 'no Power = no viable strategy' to an owner-run business that earns a fair living from execution

requirements.labor: owner 30-60 minutes for competitor and evidence notes
requirements.capability: basic competitor knowledge; voc-research or competitor-teardown output helps
requirements.measurement: retention, price vs alternatives, or cost per job if any exist

metrics: cost per unit vs rivals (if known)
guardrails: No advantage claim without a named Barrier and non-inference evidence
An execution advantage is not a failure; say so plainly
stop_review: Review when a competitor copies the edge, a new substitute appears, or retention/price evidence contradicts the claim
alternatives: No competitor data: mark Barrier 'unknown', run competitor-teardown
No customer data: run PB-interviews before asserting Benefit
frameworks.interpretation: Interpretation: the Benefit/Barrier pair maps onto book 01 section 9's four tests (customer relevance + economic compatibility = Benefit; durability = Barrier) but adds a typed Barrier and a per-competitor check, which is what makes a durability claim testable. Most small businesses will land on 'execution advantage' and that is a valid plan basis.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed: an advantage or moat claim in a plan must name its Barrier type, the competitor it holds against, and at least one non-inference evidence item; otherwise label it execution advantage or unknown
proposed: never tell an owner the business has 'no viable strategy' because no Power was found; state that growth rests on copyable execution and size commitments accordingly
proposed: assess advantage per strategically separate offer (e.g. an agency's retainer vs its one-off audits) rather than for the whole firm

frameworks.climbos_location: skills/growth-strategy/SKILL.md (new step after diagnosis); shared/agents/decision.ts DecisionSchema (new advantage field); skills/competitor-teardown/SKILL.md

relation_to_existing.note: Candidate v2 of the book 01 advantage review: same four tests, plus typed Barrier and per-competitor relativity. Extends BK01's 'name the advantage growth comes from' with a test for whether the advantage is durable.

frameworks.disagreements: Book 01 scores durability as one of four tests; Helmer says Benefits are common and the Barrier decides. Helmer also implies any business without Power lacks a strategy; book 01 and BK01 treat execution and focus as legitimate bases for small firms. Decide by goal: for owner-income plans, Power is a bonus; for plans that justify heavy upfront spend or long payback, a named Barrier should be required.

frameworks.name: Small-business Power availability map
frameworks.decision: Which of the seven Power types are worth considering for this business, and which to rule out fast
evidence_required: business type and geography
cost structure (fixed vs variable)
whether customers buy again or buy add-ons
any exclusive asset: lease, licence, supplier deal, data, patent
years operating in same niche

branches.if: route-based local service (lawn, pest, cleaning, pool)
branches.then: consider bounded Scale Economies via route density in chosen neighbourhoods; plan acquisition by area cluster

branches.if: recurring service, SaaS with stored data or workflows, agency or accountant relationship
branches.then: consider Switching Costs; build follow-on offers and genuine embedding (see K5)

branches.if: challenger whose incumbents profit from a practice customers dislike
branches.then: consider Counter-Positioning (see K4)

branches.if: an exclusive asset obtained on terms not priced at its value
branches.then: run the five Cornered Resource tests; founder skill usually fails 'sufficient' and 'non-arbitraged'

branches.if: marketplace or community
branches.then: Network Economies only if bounded network can tip locally and benefit is material; otherwise treat as a channel

branches.if: young business or B2B buyer focused on specs
branches.then: rule out Branding and Process Power as near-term Powers; reputation and process are Benefits

steps: Rule out types that don't fit the stage and model
For each remaining type, state industry economics (is the effect strong in this niche?) and competitive position (are we ahead?) separately
Keep at most 3 candidates
Attach a test or evidence task to each
exceptions_failure_modes: Copying Netflix/Intel scale logic to a firm with no fixed-cost lead
Confusing awareness with Branding (big ad budgets are scale, not brand)
Treating reviews as a Barrier (rivals can accumulate reviews too)
Calling a key person a Cornered Resource

requirements.labor: owner input on costs and assets
requirements.measurement: cost per job or per account, repeat or add-on rate

metrics: cost per job by area (route businesses)
share of new customers in target cluster
guardrails: Large-company cases are illustrations, not small-business rules
Industry economics and competitive position judged separately; both must be positive
stop_review: Re-run when the business changes model, geography or adds a recurring offer
alternatives: No cost data: skip scale analysis, mark unknown
No competitor data: map only own-side candidates and mark position unknown
frameworks.interpretation: Interpretation (not Helmer's claims): realistic for small firms are bounded Scale Economies (route density, niche-leading fixed-cost tools), Switching Costs, Counter-Positioning against larger or legacy incumbents, and occasional Cornered Resources (exclusive lease, scarce licence, proprietary data). Mostly out of reach: Network Economies outside small bounded marketplaces, Branding in Helmer's strict sense (decades; B2B rarely), Process Power (rare even for giants).

proposed_rules.rule: proposed: the plan considers at most 3 candidate Power types and states why the others are ruled out in one line each
proposed: don't project a brand price premium within a 90-day plan; treat brand work as a conversion Benefit
proposed: a Cornered Resource claim must pass the five tests (idiosyncratic, non-arbitraged, transferable, ongoing, sufficient), recorded per test

frameworks.climbos_location: skills/growth-strategy/SKILL.md; skills/plays-local/SKILL.md (route-density note); skills/positioning/SKILL.md (differentiator vs Power note)

relation_to_existing.note: No existing library text maps Power types to small-business models.

frameworks.disagreements: Helmer treats B2B Branding as weak; for small local trades, uncertainty-reduction reputation can earn a modest premium. Decide on the owner's own price-vs-competitor evidence, not the book.

frameworks.name: Power Progression stage check (what to build now)
frameworks.decision: Whether to prioritise acquisition, switching costs, business-model choices or protection right now, based on stage and market flux
evidence_required: customer or unit growth over 12 months with the starting base
market flux signals: new regulation, new technology, new area, shortage, new category
whether buyers ask 'who can do this?' or compare prices
retention and repeat data

branches.if: origination (no compelling value yet, little or no traction)
branches.then: focus on the offer and business model: Counter-Positioning choice, securing any exclusive resource; acquisition only as learning tests

branches.if: takeoff signals: market in flux and buyers asking 'can I get it?'
branches.then: prioritise capturing installed base with genuine switching costs (contracts, embedded workflows, follow-on offers) and fast execution; acquisition spend still under owner's cash and payback guardrails

branches.if: stability: buyers compare deals, rivals know customer value
branches.then: don't buy share on lock-in assumptions; protect and deepen existing customers (follow-on offers, price review), improve process and reputation over years

branches.if: growth from a small base only (e.g. 10 to 20 customers) with no market flux signal
branches.then: stage unknown; treat as origination/stability for spending purposes

steps: Compute 12-month unit growth in code and keep the base
Collect market flux signals separately from own growth
Pick the stage, or 'unknown'
List the Power types whose window is open at that stage (max 3)
Set the quarter's emphasis: model / installed base / protection
exceptions_failure_modes: Reading 100% growth from a tiny base as market takeoff
Using the 30-40% cutoff as a law
Confusing the stage with product life-cycle stages
Taking strong margins in a boom as proof of Power

requirements.cash: depends on branch; takeoff branch may justify front-loaded but capped spend
requirements.measurement: unit growth with base, retention, attach rate

metrics: share of new customers on contracts or follow-on offers
guardrails: Stage is a labelled heuristic, never a computed certainty
Takeoff never overrides cash floor, capacity or payback guardrails
stop_review: Review each quarter or when growth slows sharply; a boom ending is the moment arbitrage arrives
alternatives: No growth data: ask for customer counts 12 months ago and now
No market signals: default to stability rules for spending
frameworks.interpretation: Interpretation: for small firms the most usable part is the buyer-question proxy ('can I get it?' vs 'best deal?') and the barrier timing, not the 30-40% number, which was set for large markets. Small businesses rarely see true takeoff; local versions occur with new regulations, new housing areas or new platforms.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed: compute stage only when the 12-month starting base is at least a minimum count (owner-configurable; e.g. 30 customers); otherwise stage = unknown
proposed: when stage is stability or unknown, affordable CAC must not include unobserved lock-in lifetimes
proposed: in a takeoff branch, prefer plays that convert new customers onto recurring or embedded arrangements over one-off sales

frameworks.climbos_location: shared/agents/diagnosis.ts (optional stage reading); skills/growth-strategy/SKILL.md; shared/agents/economics.ts (no change, guardrail reference)

relation_to_existing.note: Adds a timing view to BK01's 'riding market growth' trap and supports the skill's rule to extend value only with own repeat data.

frameworks.disagreements: Helmer frames takeoff as a race where share must be won; growth-strategy SKILL and book 01 favour bounded, reversible tests. Decide by evidence of market flux and cash: without both, ClimbOS's guardrails win.

frameworks.name: Counter-Positioning test for small challengers
frameworks.decision: Whether a different business model will be left alone by incumbents, and against whom it protects
evidence_required: incumbents' business model: pricing unit, fees, contract terms, channel
how much incumbent revenue depends on the practice the new model removes
the new model's own margin at a realistic volume
which similar small rivals could copy the new model and what they would lose
prerequisites: unit economics of the new model computed in code

branches.if: new model is profitable on its own AND a named incumbent would lose material revenue by copying
branches.then: Counter-Positioning against that incumbent; plan expects a delayed response, not none

branches.if: new model unattractive on its own
branches.then: not Counter-Positioning; incumbent simply sees a bad business

branches.if: competitors have little revenue tied to the old practice
branches.then: not Counter-Positioning; it is a copyable differentiator

branches.if: Counter-Positioning holds vs incumbent but similar challengers can copy freely
branches.then: partial; plan needs another Benefit/Barrier vs like rivals (switching costs, density, reputation)

steps: List top incumbents' models
Find the revenue they would put at risk by copying
Compute the new model's standalone margin
Check like-model rivals separately
Write the hook only after the tests pass
Set a review trigger for incumbent response
exceptions_failure_modes: Assuming 'they can't copy' when the rival is a small shop that can change prices overnight
Ignoring that collateral damage shrinks as the challenger grows
Loud attacks on the incumbent that speed its response
Below-cost launch pricing without a loss ceiling

requirements.cash: launch pricing losses, if any, capped and approved
requirements.measurement: new model margin; share of new customers switching from the named incumbent

guardrails: Comparative claims must be true and sourced (claims ledger)
Below-cost pricing only as an owner-approved, capped experiment
stop_review: Incumbent adopts the model in a segment: re-run K1 for that competitor
Standalone margin falls below owner floor
alternatives: No incumbent revenue data: mark collateral damage unknown and present the model as a differentiator
Owner can't afford launch pricing: launch at normal margin
frameworks.interpretation: Interpretation: for small firms the incumbent is often a regional chain, franchise or legacy provider with fee income; small local peers rarely face collateral damage, so the same model gives no protection against them.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed: label a model 'counter-position' only if both the standalone-margin test and the named-incumbent collateral-damage test pass; else 'differentiator'
proposed: every counter-position names the like-model rivals it does not protect against
proposed: comparative hooks about competitors' fees or terms must be verified current facts

relation_to_existing.note: Existing procedure (built from a secondary summary) has the cannibalisation idea and a margin check, but lacks the standalone test, the like-rival limit and the shrinking-damage dynamic. Candidate v2.

frameworks.disagreements: The existing library lists 'flat pricing vs hourly billers' and 'no-contract vs annual lock-in' as counter-positions; under Helmer's test these are only counter-positions where the competitor earns materially from the old practice. Decide per competitor with revenue-at-risk evidence.

frameworks.name: Switching costs through follow-on value (not traps)
frameworks.decision: Whether to invest in follow-on offers and genuine embedding with existing customers before (or instead of) more acquisition
evidence_required: existence of follow-on purchases (renewals, add-ons, repeat jobs)
current attach or repeat rate
what customers would lose by leaving (data, setup, training, relationships)
retention data
prerequisites: some paying customers; retention not broken

branches.if: follow-on purchases exist and attach rate is low
branches.then: build one follow-on offer (maintenance plan, add-on service, annual plan) and measure attach

branches.if: no follow-on purchases are possible (one-off product)
branches.then: switching costs give no Benefit; focus elsewhere (referrals, conversion)

branches.if: proposal raises switching costs by making leaving harder rather than staying more valuable
branches.then: reject; propose genuine embedding instead

branches.if: retention is weak
branches.then: fix retention first (PB-lifecycle-email, PB-activation-repair) before adding offers

steps: List follow-on purchases
Classify current switching costs: financial, procedural, relational
Pick one value-adding follow-on offer
Measure attach rate and retention of attached customers
Review pricing for embedded customers with notice (PB-price-increase)
exceptions_failure_modes: Dark patterns: hidden cancellation, blocked data export, surprise auto-renewal
Assuming lock-in justifies higher acquisition spend in a mature market
Adding many add-ons that fragment delivery capacity

requirements.capability: service or product able to deliver the follow-on
requirements.measurement: attach rate, retention by attached vs not

guardrails: Customers can always leave and take their data
Price changes to existing customers only with notice and owner approval
Renewal and cancellation terms clear and lawful where the business operates
stop_review: Attach rate flat after 8 weeks: revise offer
alternatives: No customers yet: not applicable; use origination plays
frameworks.interpretation: Interpretation: this is the most broadly available Power for small firms, but Helmer's own point that the benefit is competed away at acquisition in mature markets means it supports retention and pricing of current customers more than acquisition. The ethics guardrail is ClimbOS policy, not Helmer.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed: never recommend raising switching costs by restricting exit (blocked export, hidden cancellation)
proposed: when a business has follow-on purchases and attach rate under its own target, rank a follow-on offer play ahead of new acquisition plays of similar cost
proposed: switching-cost claims do not raise affordable CAC unless observed retention supports the longer lifetime

frameworks.climbos_location: skills/retention-lifecycle/SKILL.md; candidate playbook PB-follow-on-offer in shared/playbooks/contracts.ts (check overlap with BRP-03 package architecture)

relation_to_existing.note: Existing library treats switching cost as a buyer objection to overcome; this adds the seller-side view, with BK02's anti-trapping ethics.

frameworks.disagreements: Helmer describes SAP's ability to raise prices on locked-in, unhappy clients as a Benefit; ClimbOS should not recommend exploiting dissatisfied captive customers. Policy decides.

frameworks.name: Advantage ledger: name where growth comes from
frameworks.decision: What advantage the plan's growth rests on, and how that changes spend sizing
evidence_required: K1 result
BK01 growth source class (advantage share gain / market tide / substitution / bought / extension)
concentration of current customer sources

branches.if: a Power with evidence
branches.then: plan names it; at least one play deepens or protects the Barrier (e.g. follow-on offer, density cluster)

branches.if: execution advantage only
branches.then: plan says so; spend sized to short payback; one play aims to build a Barrier over time

branches.if: growth from market tide
branches.then: flag margin-after-slowdown risk (false-positive Power)

branches.if: unknown
branches.then: first-week task collects competitor and retention evidence

steps: Fill advantage: type, Benefit, Barrier, competitor it holds against, evidence, stage
Classify growth source
Tag each play: uses advantage / builds Barrier / execution only
Check spend sizing vs advantage type
exceptions_failure_modes: Generic 'our AI is our moat' text
Listing a Power with only inference evidence
Ignoring a dominant referral source that a partner could redirect
metrics: share of plans with evidenced advantage field
share of plays tagged to build a Barrier
guardrails: No invented competitors or competitor facts
alternatives: Flag off: keep current decision contract; advantage noted in limits
frameworks.interpretation: Interpretation: BK01 asks 'what advantage does growth come from?'; Helmer supplies the test for whether that advantage lasts. The Fundamental Equation is used only qualitatively: a play grows market reach (M) or protects share/margin (s, m), never as a computed valuation.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed: the decision contract gains an advantage field (type, barrier, competitor, evidence source, stage); type 'none_yet' is valid
proposed: lint warns when plan text claims a moat, network effect or lock-in that is not recorded in the advantage field with non-inference evidence
proposed: when advantage is none_yet or unknown, plays requiring payback beyond the plan's guardrail are blocked

relation_to_existing.note: Candidate v2 of BK01's 'growth must name its advantage' rule, with a durability test. The 01_strategy guide's StrategyDecision has no advantage field (BK01 review G10 already flagged this).

frameworks.disagreements: None with BK01; tension with growth-strategy SKILL's ambition section (volume engines) only if advantage is none and spend is large. Guardrails decide.

frameworks.name: 'Me too won't do': invention path and commitment sizing
frameworks.decision: Whether to copy a competitor's offer cheaper, or invent a different offer, and how big a commitment to make
evidence_required: the proposed offer vs competitors
whether the customer need is known
the margin impact of any price cut
cash available for the commitment

branches.if: plan is 'same offer, lower price' in a market where rivals can match
branches.then: show the volume needed to keep contribution; expect matching; prefer a differentiated offer test

branches.if: capabilities-led (we can build X, need unproven)
branches.then: small staged commitments; stay in the game; look for an early Barrier

branches.if: customer-led (need known, solution hard)
branches.then: the risk is delivery; test feasibility first

branches.if: competitor-led (beat an existing offer)
branches.then: needs a clearly better whole offer and complements lined up; larger commitment only with owner approval

steps: Classify the path
Compute price-cut break-even volume in code if relevant
Size the commitment to path risk
Set a review date
exceptions_failure_modes: Price war against a larger rival
Big upfront spend on an unproven capability bet
Treating the 10x rule as universal
stop_review: Volume below break-even by review date: stop the price cut
alternatives: No cash for commitments: concierge test (PB-concierge)
frameworks.interpretation: Interpretation: for small firms 'invention' usually means a new offer, package or business model, not technology. Helmer's call for crafting through experiments matches book 01 section 12 sequencing.

proposed_rules.rule: proposed: a 'match competitor at lower price' play must show break-even volume and the expected rival response
proposed: capabilities-led bets start as capped tests with a stated learning goal
